The keeper's log

A short story · 6 minute read

The tide tables were wrong again on Tuesday. Mara checked them twice, then a third time, and the numbers still disagreed with the water lapping at the second step of the slipway.

She wrote the discrepancy in the log, in pencil, because pencil survives a soaking. The log was older than she was. Its first pages were in a hand nobody could read any more, and its last pages were hers.

The keeper's rule was simple: write down what you see, not what you expected to see. Every keeper before her had copied it onto the inside cover, and every one of them had broken it at least once.

At dusk she climbed the hundred and twelve steps, trimmed the wick, polished the lens with the soft cloth that lived in the drawer, and lit the lamp. The lamp did not care about tide tables. The lamp cared about oil, and about being lit on time.

By noon the next day the harbour master had heard about the tables, and by one o'clock the whole quay knew. Nobody blamed the tables. Everybody blamed the moon, which was easier, and which could not answer back.

That evening a trawler came in late, low in the water, its skipper shouting that the channel had moved. Mara went down with the lamp and the log, and stood on the slipway writing while the men argued about sandbanks.

Her own mistake had come in her first winter: a ship she had been sure was there, a light she had been sure she saw. She had written it down. In the morning there had been nothing on the water, and nothing in any other keeper's log.

She left the entry in. Crossing it out would have been a second mistake on top of the first, and the log was not for her.
